panels.title: Node CPU Commit %

panels.description:
% of each node guaranteed to pods on it.

When this hits 100%, the autoscaler will spawn a new node and the scheduler will stop
putting pods on the old node.
panels.title: Node Memory Commit %

panels.description:
% of CPU in each node pool guaranteed to user workloads.

Most commonly, JupyterHub workloads are *memory bound*, not CPU bound. So this is
not a particularly helpful graph.

Common shapes this visualization may take:
1. If this is *consistently high* but shaped differently than your memory commitment
  graph, consider changing your CPU requirements.
panels.title: Node Pool CPU commitment %

panels.description:
% of memory in each node pool guaranteed to user workloads.

Common shapes this visualization may take:
1. If this is consistently low (<50%), you are paying for cloud compute that you do not
  need. Consider reducing the size of your nodes, or increasing the amount of
  memory guaranteed to your users. Some variability based on time of day is to be expected.
panels.title: Node Pool Memory commitment %

panels.description:
Pods in states other than 'Running', per node pool of the node they are scheduled on.

Pending pods that have not been scheduled to a node yet are shown as 'unscheduled'.
Unscheduled placeholder pods are shown separately in grey: they are evicted to make room for users and wait for the autoscaler by design, so long grey bars are normal. Unscheduled user pods are what the 'Pods unschedulable' alert watches.
Filter with the Node pool and Pod status selectors.

targets.expr:
sum by (label_cloud_google_com_gke_nodepool, phase) (
  (kube_pod_status_phase{phase!="Running", phase=~"$status"} == 1)
  * on (namespace, pod, uid) group_left(node) topk by (namespace, pod, uid) (1, kube_pod_info{node!=""})
  * on (node) group_left(label_cloud_google_com_gke_nodepool) group by (node, label_cloud_google_com_gke_nodepool) (kube_node_labels{label_cloud_google_com_gke_nodepool=~"$nodepool"})
)
